title: Beef Bourguignon
description:
According to Julia Child, Beef Bourguignon “is certainly one of the most delicious beef dishes concocted by man.” We certainly agree and are working from her recipe from “Mastering the Art of French Cooking,” the book that changed the way America cooks.
I got to eat with Julia once (I was her escort), at a dinner with Stan Calderwood, my boss at Trinity and a good friend of Julia’s. It was here that she taught me to enjoy a “very wet Martini.” (In case you’re wondering, Julia’s wet Martini is the opposite of a classic dry Martini, with virtually no Vermouth and almost all Gin, or Vodka. Julia’s started with a wide-mouthed wine glass filled with ice, then had Vermouth poured over it almost to the top, and finally had Gin floated along the top – not stirred or shaken – and much less alcoholic than the usual Martini.)
Back to the Beef Bourguignon: this is not only classic French cuisine, but classic “comfort food.”
START TO FINISH: 3 HOURS
Beef Bourguignon
Sauté the bacon in the oil over moderate heat for 3 to 5 minutes. Remove to a side dish, leaving the bacon fat in the pan.
Return the beef and bacon to the casserole with the vegetables and toss with a teaspoon of salt and some pepper. Then sprinkle on the 2 tablespoons of flour.
Set the casserole uncovered in the middle position of the preheated oven for 4 minutes. Toss the meat around and return to the oven for 4 minutes more. (This browns the flour and covers the meat with a light crust.)
Remove the casserole and turn the oven down to 325 degrees.
ingredients: 3 pounds beef, thickly cut, like chuck or rump pot roast
2-3 cups (bottle) of good solid drinking wine, could be a Chianti
1 pound sliced mushrooms, like Portobellos butter parsley springs, chopped
directions: Cut the beef into thick cubes, 1 to 2 inches, and dry with paper towels; it won’t brown if it’s damp.
Sauté the beef, a few pieces at a time, in the hot oil and bacon fat until nicely browned on all sides, 5-7 minutes. Move the browned pieces to the dish with the bacon.
In the same fat, brown the chopped vegetables, 5-7 minutes. Pour out the fat.
While the beef is cooking, sauté the mushrooms in some butter until nicely browned, 7-10 minutes.
Similarly, sauté the carrots in a little butter until browned, 7-10 minutes.

For the onions, I usually use frozen pearl onions because they’re peeled and ready to go. Add a little water and a little butter to a small pan and heat the onions over moderately high heat until the water evaporates and then the onions get a nice brown color, around 10 minutes.
When the beef is tender (about 2 ½ hours), carefully take the meat out and keep warm. Strain the casserole liquid through a sieve into a saucepan. Skim off any fat in the sauce.
You can pick on the casserole-cooked vegetables, grind them up in a food processor with a little sauce and push what fits through a fine sieve, or toss them out.
Check the sauce for consistency – it should be silky and smooth – adding more broth or water if too thick or thickening it by boiling it down a bit. Also check for salt and pepper.
Add the sautéed vegetables to the sauce and heat for a few minutes, allowing the vegetables to soak up some of the sauce flavors.
Then pour it all over the beef.
Serve with potatoes or noodles, garnished with chopped parsley.
Stir in the wine and enough beef stock so that the meat is barely covered. Add the tomato paste, garlic, thyme, and bay leaf.
Bring to a simmer on top of the stove. Then cover the casserole and set in the lower third of the oven (now 325 degrees).
Regulate the heat so the liquid simmers very slowly for about 2 ½ hours. The meat should be fork tender when done.
